sections.title: 1. History Taking & Interview Skills: tasks and non-directive techniques

blocks.text: The four tasks of a psychiatric interview are: 1. build a therapeutic alliance; 2. obtain the demographic information required; 3. interview for diagnosis; 4. negotiate a treatment plan.

Approaching threatening topics: (1) use normalizing questions to decrease the patient's sense of embarrassment about a feeling or behaviour; (2) use symptom expectation and reduction of guilt to defuse admission of embarrassing behaviour; (3) use symptom exaggeration to determine the actual frequency of a sensitive or shameful behaviour; (4) use familiar language when asking about behaviours.

**EMI** matches for interview techniques: 'I'd like to hear more about your parents, but first let me get a picture of what's happening to you of late' (after the patient changes topic) is **REDIRECTION**; 'Sometimes when people are very depressed, they think of hurting themselves. Has this been true for you?' is **NORMALISATION** (the interviewer phrases the question so the patient realises they are not the only person with such thoughts, making a taboo topic easier to explore); 'What sorts of drugs do you usually use when you're drinking?' is **SYMPTOM** **EXPECTATION**; 'I can see that you look anxious when talking about those voices' is **ACKNOWLEDGEMENT**; the clinician describing their own **fluoxetine** side effects is **SELF-REVELATION**, which can powerfully backfire and is not recommended unless necessary for engagement.

blocks.title: Non-directive techniques
rows: Opening stage of the interview, to allow free narration; non-directive technique
Preferable when highly suggestible; not very useful to focus if over-talkative or extremely poor historian. Usually starts with 'tell me', 'describe', etc.
Repeating the exact words of the patient
Pt: I was having bad dreams last night. Dr: So, you were having bad dreams last night.
Helps patient to feel that doctor is listening actively
Similar to repetition but phrases rearranged
Pt: I was having bad dreams last night. Dr: So, you are getting disturbed by the dreams you have.
Helps patient to feel that doctor is listening actively
Brief summarisation of what the patient has said up to a point in the interview
'So from what you have told so far, you are worried for last 4 months and not sleeping well, and your job is at risk. Right?'
Helps patient to check if he has said what he intended to say. Helps the doctor to form an idea of the narration so far.
Doctor tries to get details from patients about what the patient has already said
'You said you are feeling depressed ever since you can remember. When do you feel most depressed?'
Helps in avoiding misconceptions by the clinician. Also shows clinician's interest in knowing more.
Helping patients continue the interview by providing both verbal and nonverbal encouragement
Approval nods, leaning forward slightly to express interest, 'Yes. And then?', 'yeah, go on...', 'Uh-huh' etc.
Helps patient to feel that doctor is listening actively. Encourages flow of information.

blocks.text: Open questions are **MORE** **INFORMATIVE** - not time-saving, doctor-directed, reliable or less precise: an open question does not suggest the possible answer while a closed question expects a limited range of replies, so begin with open questions and turn to closed ones only to clarify details or factual points.

blocks.text: **SUGGESTIVE** questions are the odd one out among techniques that facilitate disclosure (silence, positive reinforcement, acknowledgement of affect and validation do facilitate): the answer is contained in the question itself, which misleads both patient and doctor and leaves the patient little choice but to agree.

blocks.text: **EMI** named-technique matches: 'What brings you to the clinic today?' is an **OPEN-ENDED** question (cannot be answered yes/no); asking when the patient feels most depressed after 'low mood ever since you can remember' is **CLARIFICATION**; 'So, you are getting disturbed by the dreams you have' is **RESTATEMENT** (phrases rearranged); 'So, you were having bad dreams last night' is **REPETITION** (the patient's exact words); 'So from what you told so far, you are anxious... Right?' is **SUMMATION**, which lets the patient clarify or modify the doctor's understanding.

blocks.note: Not in the notes: a linking statement is a type of reflective statement, a helpful non-directive approach, in which the interviewer links feelings to experiences and behaviours ('you feel [feeling] because [experience or behaviour that gave rise to the feeling]'); the question keys it over restricted affect, frequent interpretations, long pauses and polythematic questions.

bullets.text: Four tasks of the interview: build alliance, get demographics, interview for diagnosis, negotiate a treatment plan.
Threatening topics: normalizing questions, symptom expectation, symptom exaggeration, familiar language.
Open-ended questions open the interview and allow free narration; preferable when highly suggestible; poor use if over-talkative or extremely poor historian.
Repetition repeats the patient's exact words; restatement rearranges the phrasing; both show the doctor is listening actively.
Summation briefly summarises what the patient has said so far, letting the patient check it and helping the doctor form an idea of the narration.
Clarification seeks details of what the patient already said; facilitation uses verbal and nonverbal encouragement ('uh-huh', nods) to keep information flowing.

sections.title: 2. Directive techniques and changing topics

blocks.text: Non-directive techniques are employed without focussing on a particular answer. Directive techniques are focussed on seeking a particular answer or driven by other motives of the doctor; they are not necessarily detrimental but must be used judiciously.

Techniques when changing topics: (1) smooth transitions hint at something the patient just said; (2) referred transitions hint at something said earlier in the interview; (3) introduced transitions pull a new topic from thin air.

**REFERRED** transition = referring back to something the patient said **EARLIER** in the interview to move to a new topic (keyed over sudden, smooth, introduced transition and distraction technique); the explanation says it is often used to 'come back' to a topic of importance.

blocks.title: Directive techniques
rows: When, where, how many, which and what questions. Answers can only be 'yes or no' in most occasions. When clubbed with non-facilitative gestures can be detrimental to the interview process. Stating a presumption followed by tags can be very directive.
'Did you sleep well last night?'; 'You have lost weight. Haven't you?'

Better avoided in early parts of the interview as they can produce prescribed answers lacking in detail. Also avoid in highly suggestible patients. Good technique is to start with open; move to closed by the end of the interview. Useful to rule out less likely symptoms.
Persisting with a question to seek an answer; restating the question in different terms for a second time
Often used when patient digresses from the topic of discussion. The motive is to collect the specific information.
Gently reorienting patient towards the topic of discussion
Pt: 'It is not good if one's parents are divorced even before one goes to school.' Doc: 'I'd like to hear more about your parents, but first let me get a picture of what's happening to you of late'.
The motive is to keep the patient on track.
Moving from one to another topic; a special skill, preferably done as smoothly as possible to keep the patient interested
'You mentioned that your mother is a medical secretary. What about yourself? What job do you do?'
Smooth transitions use the cue off something the patient just said. Referred transitions use the cue off something said earlier in the interview. Introduced transitions use a new topic to proceed.
Useful to manage time pressure, especially in garrulous patients
'I am going to interrupt you as there are few important things we need to cover today'.
To be used cautiously, overuse may detach patient from the doctor. The motive is to use time effectively.

blocks.text: Closed questions are useful when the patient is distracted or over-talkative, in the later part of the interview and to rule out less likely symptoms - the keyed answer is 'All of the listed options'. The explanation still warns that closed questions are better avoided early and in highly suggestible patients: start open, then go closed.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

bullets.text: Directive techniques seek a particular answer; not necessarily detrimental but must be used judiciously.
Three transitions: smooth (cue from what the patient just said), referred (cue from earlier in the interview), introduced (new topic from thin air).
Closed questions: yes/no answers; avoid early and in highly suggestible patients; start open and move to closed by the end; useful to rule out less likely symptoms.
Question rephrasing restates the question in different terms to collect specific information when the patient digresses.
Redirection gently reorients the patient to the topic to keep them on track.
Limit setting manages time pressure in garrulous patients; overuse may detach the patient from the doctor.

sections.title: 3. Other methods to elicit information

blocks.title: Other methods to elicit information
rows: Point out to a patient something to which the doctor thinks the patient is missing or denying
'You seem not to have gained any weight in last 6 months. Is it possible that your eating has been poor again?'
Must be done in a respectful way. The aim is to help patients face a difficult aspect rather than dismissing patients by showing a negative aspect.
Clarifying certain associations or relationships that the patient may not see
'You seem very anxious when talking about your job. Are you having any problems at workplace?'
Sophisticated technique and should generally be used only after the doctor has established some rapport. Should be stated as a hypothesis after sufficient collection of evidence from the interview.
'Do you like Shakespeare? I was a mad fan when I was at school.'
Helps physician feel at ease sometimes. Excessive self-revelation is a boundary violation.
Silence can be used either to facilitate discourse or to indicate disapproval or disinterest
Sometimes useful and allows free emotional expression. Relieves patient's pressure and he/she may feel relaxed that not every moment must be spent talking.
Without a formal admission from the patient, asking about details of problem behaviour. Doctor assumes (rightly) that the patient is involved in the act.
'What sorts of drugs do you usually use when you're drinking?' (assuming that the patient uses drugs)
Defuse the admission of embarrassing behaviour. May help in reduction of guilt. But must be used with experience and according to the context.
When deception or minimisation is expected, overstating a guessed frequency in order to elicit a true answer
'How many times have you taken overdoses since your last hospitalization? Four? Five?'
Also helpful in reducing guilt to certain extent as the patient feels that the doctor has expected a higher amount of problem than what she/he actually has brought.

blocks.text: Confrontation is used to help the patient **FACE** a difficult aspect of their problems - pointing out something the doctor thinks the patient is missing or denying, done respectfully rather than dismissing the patient by pointing out a negative aspect. 'Clarify certain associations that patients may not see' is a distractor (the notes give that description to interpretation).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **EMI** named-technique matches: 'You seem not to have gained any weight in the last three months. Is it possible that your eating has been poor again?' is **CONFRONTATION**; 'I am going to interrupt you as there are few important things we need to cover today' is **LIMIT** **SETTING**; 'Did you sleep well last night?' is a **CLOSED** question; 'Do you like Sir Cliff Richards? I was a mad fan while at school' is **SELF-REVELATION**; 'You mentioned that your mother is a receptionist. What about yourself?' is a **TRANSITION**.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/EMIS all chapters/EMIs Clinical Examination.pdf

bullets.text: Confrontation points out what the doctor thinks the patient is missing or denying; done respectfully to help the patient face a difficult aspect.
Interpretation clarifies associations the patient may not see; sophisticated, used after rapport, stated as a hypothesis.
Self-revelation is limited discreet self-disclosure; excessive self-revelation is a boundary violation.
Silence can facilitate discourse or indicate disapproval/disinterest; allows free emotional expression.
Symptom expectation: ask about details assuming the patient is involved in the behaviour, to defuse admission and reduce guilt.
Symptom exaggeration: overstate a guessed frequency when deception/minimisation is expected, to elicit the true answer.

sections.title: 4. Supportive and obstructive techniques

blocks.title: Supportive techniques - not aimed at eliciting information
rows: Used to instil positive hope and avoid or reduce despair. Must not be falsely reassuring.
'The depression may be very difficult for you. I think it is very likely with the proper treatment you can get back to your job'.
Many patients seek advice directly; it is acceptable to provide advice but based on sound understanding of the context. Premature advice can be obstructive rather than facilitative.
'I think it is best for you to consider **ECT** at this time. If I am you, I will give this a serious thought.'
Conscious and deliberate postponement of delicate issues; but must be opened at an appropriate time.
'I can see that you are uneasy to tell me about your relationships. That's **OK**, we can come back to this when you feel ready to discuss with me.'
Helps to decrease a patient's sense of embarrassment about a feeling or behaviour. Generally done by quoting how it is normal for people to have different emotions/reactions/behaviours, etc.
'Sometimes when people are very depressed, they think of hurting themselves. Has this been true for you?'
Making a remark about patient's affect can facilitate disclosure.
'I can see that you look anxious when talking about those voices.'
Gently uplifting self-esteem by statements of praise (but at a realistic extent)
'Well, I think you've described the situation in a way that helped me understand what you have been going through'.
Affirmative statements (must be genuine and appropriate) indicating respect and dignity along with positive reinforcement
'You have been through a lot.' 'I'm impressed at how you have hung in there.' 'You must be a very strong person.'
The interviewer encourages the patient to ask questions and to express any concerns, encouraging team working
'I'm here to help.' 'Let's plan on working on this together.'

blocks.title: Obstructive techniques that may hamper information sharing
rows: Answers are contained in the question itself. Misleads both the patient and the doctor. The patient is left with little choice.
'These voices are not from your head. Am I right?'
These questions ask the patient to discover their own problems, in a way. Not useful when used to elicit information from a distressed patient.
'Why do you keep waking up so early in the morning?'
Adding two or more questions in a single statement. This confuses the patient and will lead to either a vague response or non-response.
'Do you take a vacation every year, and are you able to relax?'
Facial expression, body posture, and behaviour that indicate lack of interest or inattentiveness
The doctor is yawning or repeatedly checking his/her watch, other repetitive gestures like tapping the table, etc.
Expressing unhappiness with a topic that the patient wants to discuss; may lead to withdrawal and not revealing the important problem faced by the patient.
Patient: 'Over the last month I have had trouble with sex'. Dr: 'We are here to talk about your sleep.'
Tricking the patient using his own words. Often seen as doctor's attempt to negate patient's problems.
'You wanted to see me as nothing had gone well for you, but you just said that you have got a new job and keeping a good shape.'

blocks.mnemonic: Silly Wise Clinicians Never Deliver Success

blocks.text: **VALIDATION** is the supportive technique that is not aimed at eliciting information (keyed over clarification, redirection, interpretation and symptom expectation): it decreases a patient's sense of embarrassment about a feeling or behaviour, often by quoting how it is normal for people to have different emotions, reactions and behaviours.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: 'I am impressed by what you have achieved despite all these difficulties' is a **RESPECTFUL** **STATEMENT** (keyed over summation, inquiry, facilitation and reflection): it conveys the mutual respect maintained by the therapist after an emotionally important disclosure and can facilitate further conversation.

Praising a patient who stopped part-way through narrating her job problems for doing well despite a difficult time is keyed **REINFORCEMENT** (not validation, acknowledgment of affect, setting traps or a suggestive lead): the explanation stresses that without reinforcement the interview becomes less productive.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

bullets.text: Supportive (not information-eliciting): reassurance, advice, postponement, validation/normalisation, acknowledgement of affect, positive reinforcement, statement of respect, partnering.
Reassurance must not be falsely reassuring; premature advice can obstruct rather than facilitate.
Validation/normalisation quotes how normal different reactions are, to decrease embarrassment.
Statement of respect = genuine affirmative statements indicating respect and dignity with positive reinforcement.
Partnering: invite the patient's questions and concerns, encouraging team working.
Obstructive: suggestive, why and compound questions, negative nonverbal gestures, disapproval, setting traps.
Suggestive questions contain the answer in the question; compound questions confuse and give vague or no response.

sections.title: 5. Open vs closed questions, difficult historians, ancillary methods and interpreters

blocks.title: Open-ended vs closed-ended questions
rows: Non-reproducible at a later date, or by a different doctor
Low precision - do not focus on target symptoms
The intent of the question is clear, so precise, focused answers are elicited
Not very time efficient; may lead to circumstantial elaborations
Low, as patient selects the content revealed
Good, as doctor selects interested content

blocks.text: Techniques for a poor historian: use open-ended questions and commands to increase the flow of information; use continuation techniques to keep the flow coming; shift to neutral ground when necessary; schedule a second interview when all else fails.

Techniques for an over-talkative garrulous historian: use closed-ended and multiple-choice questions to limit the flow; perfect the art of the gentle interruption; educate the patient about the need to move along in the interview.

Behavioural observation methods: observing and recording behavioural events to study mental state or plan intervention; often used when patients are in seclusion. Event sampling: e.g. every fifth or tenth event is coded in detail. Time sampling: observations may be made only every 5 or 10 minutes.

'Functional analysis' attempts to explain and predict the functions of a phenomenon by examining any relationships to the outcome. It is a special variant of behavioural observation in which the sequence of antecedent environmental events, target behaviour, concurrent events and consequent outcomes are observed (also called **ABC** analysis); often used in **LD** settings, dementia care and challenging behaviour services.

Using an interpreter: explain the goals, structure and content of the interview to the interpreter; explain the need for literal translation (not interpreted translation) in the Mental Status Examination; ask for feedback when something is hard to translate; offer to debrief the interpreter about their own emotional concerns afterwards; ask the interpreter about the patient's degree of openness or disclosure; preferably work with the same interpreter/culture-broker for the same case.

items.text: Not a good practice with interpreters: encouraging interpretation, then translation, of the mental status examination - a literal translation is needed because a 'summarised translation' or 'interpretations' can miss salient aspects.

items.text: Multiple-choice questions are the **NOT**-a-good-technique answer for a poor historian; open-ended questions, continuation techniques (verbal and nonverbal facilitation) and shifting to neutral ground are useful.

items.text: Opening question on compliance: 'Is there any difficulty with your tablets?' - the least judgmental and least confrontational of the options offered.
Objective measures of adherence are pill counting or measuring serum or urine drug levels; sensitive questions about problems, missed doses and plans for continuation are the less direct route.
First alcohol-screening question: 'Do you enjoy a drink now and then?' - not a **CAGE** item but sensitive-interview technique: a sensitive topic is introduced gradually in a non-judgemental tone.

blocks.note: Not in the notes: the **NOT**-correct statement is 'non-invasive but direct eye contact suggests aggressiveness' - reduced eye contact may suggest passive behaviour with a lack of assertiveness, but direct eye contact does not mean aggressiveness if non-invasive, and eye contact is subject to the cultural background of therapist and patient.

Not in the notes: objective evidence of mood can be inferred from psychomotor activity, behaviour during the interview, facial reactivity and speech (tone, rate, rhythm); subjective mood can only be discerned by asking the patient how he or she feels, so the patient's stated feeling is the 'except' answer.

blocks.subtopic: Timing of the mental state examination
blocks.note: Not in the notes: the mental state examination takes place throughout the clinical interview (keyed over immediately before discussing diagnosis, during follow-up contact, immediately after presenting complaints or immediately after physical examination).

bullets.text: Open questions: highly informative but low reliability, low precision, not time efficient; closed questions: low yield but reliable, precise, time efficient.
Poor historian: open-ended questions and commands, continuation techniques, shift to neutral ground, second interview as last resort.
Garrulous historian: closed and multiple-choice questions, gentle interruption, educate about moving along.
Behavioural observation: event sampling (every 5th/10th event coded) vs time sampling (every 5 or 10 minutes); often used in seclusion.
Functional (ABC) analysis observes antecedents, behaviour and consequences; used in LD, dementia care and challenging behaviour services.
Interpreters: brief them, insist on literal (not interpreted) translation in the MSE, debrief them, use the same one for a case.

sections.title: 6. Laboratory assessment of physical factors: depression

blocks.text: Depression is a clinical diagnosis. A physical examination is always required to rule out several common medical disorders that can present with depression (especially endocrine disorders). Laboratory tests are required if medical causes are suspected and to assess baseline fitness before starting antidepressants.

Several chronic medical disorders are associated with depression (e.g. coronary artery disease, diabetes mellitus, end-stage renal disease, **HIV** infection, various malignancies, degenerative neurological disorders and stroke) but these do not 'present' with depressive features, so there is no need to exclude all of them before diagnosing depression.

blocks.title: Tests in a depression work-up
rows: Rule out infectious and inflammatory pathology
In suspected cases of sexually transmitted infections
Electrolytes, including calcium, phosphate and magnesium
Deficiency can contribute to fatigue and mimic depression
In preparation for antidepressant use and to rule out renal insufficiency contributing to depression
In preparation for antidepressant use and to rule out alcohol-related liver damage in suspected cases
In suspected cases of drug abuse
In suspected cases of Cushing disease; will require additional confirmation, as this can be positive in a large number of patients with depression
Addison's disease can also mimic depression

blocks.text: **TSH** assay is the best **SCREENING** test for subclinical hypothyroidism in a depressed woman not responding to antidepressants who is constipated and has gained weight - keyed over **T4** measurement, **T3** measurement, thyroid antibody test and thyroid scan.
None of the abnormality tests below are required routinely during a workup for depression.

**DST**-positive patients respond more favorably to biological interventions. **DST** nonsuppression is non-specific; it can be seen in chronic pain, anorexia or bulimia, alcoholism, obsessive-compulsive disorder, or anxiety disorders.

blocks.title: Other endocrine abnormalities in depression
rows: **HPA** axis abnormality in major depression results in blunted **ACTH** response to **CRH**

==1%== and ==4%== of depressed patients, especially women, show evidence of overt hypothyroidism; ==4%== to ==40%== have subclinical hypothyroidism, contributing to treatment failure. Serum **T4** reductions may accompany treatment with antidepressants, **lithium**, sleep deprivation, or **ECT**, especially in responders.
About ==30%== of depressed patients show blunted **TSH** response during depression

blocks.text: On long-term **lithium**, a **TSH** of 6.4 with a normal **T4** is subclinical thyroid disease: the keyed step is to **REPEAT** **TSH** in a month, not to add levothyroxine, reduce or stop **lithium**, or add carbimazole - the explanation says that in patients on **lithium** **TSH** must be monitored in addition to symptoms.

blocks.note: The notes mention **lithium** only as a cause of **T4** reduction; they do not list pre-**lithium** baseline investigations. **Q50** (answer: **TSH**) explains that before **lithium** one should do physical examination, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function tests, renal function, baseline weight/height (**BMI**), and if indicated **ECG** and pregnancy test.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

blocks.note: Not in the notes (they list the **ACTH** stimulation test: Addison's disease can also mimic depression): weight loss, fatigue, hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia point to Addison's disease; the explanation adds muscle weakness, fever, darkening (hyperpigmentation) of the skin including areas not exposed to the sun, and orthostatic hypotension.

blocks.subtopic: Risk factor for depression identifiable at interview
blocks.note: Not in the notes: the most prominent risk factor for depression identifiable in a clinical interview is a past history of depression (keyed over sub-average education, lack of positive life events, anxious personality traits and family history); the explanation adds that neuroticism could be a risk factor if measured with validated scales, but cross-sectional interviews are not reliable for enduring personality traits.

bullets.text: Depression is a clinical diagnosis; examine physically (especially endocrine causes); labs if medical cause suspected and for baseline before antidepressants.
Chronic medical illnesses are associated with depression but do not 'present' as it, so they need not all be excluded.
Work-up tests: FBC, TSH, B12, HIV/syphilis if suspected, electrolytes, GFR/creatinine, LFTs, toxicology; urinary free cortisol for Cushing; ACTH stimulation for Addison's.
DST non-suppression rises from grief (10%) to dysthymia (23%), MDD (44%), melancholia (50%), psychotic affective (69%) and depression with serious suicidality (78%).
DST non-suppression is non-specific (chronic pain, eating disorders, alcoholism, OCD, anxiety); DST-positive patients respond better to biological treatments.
CRH test: blunted ACTH response; TRH test: about 30% show blunted TSH response.
Overt hypothyroidism in 1-4% of depressed patients; subclinical hypothyroidism in 4-40%, contributing to treatment failure.

sections.title: 7. Laboratory assessment: anxiety and other neuroses, lactate infusion and narcoanalysis

blocks.text: A number of medical disorders can directly contribute to anxiety and panic attacks, but patients seeking clinical consultations seldom require specific investigations to diagnose them. Diagnostic possibilities for panic attacks include paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, pulmonary embolus, seizure disorder, Meniere's disease, transient ischemic attack, carcinoid syndrome, Cushing's disease, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia, and pheochromocytoma.
A physical examination is warranted for all first presentations of anxiety; extensive medical evaluation is indicated only when other features suggest physical disease.

Poor response to anxiolytic agents is the cue to look for a **MEDICAL** cause of recurrent anxiety; the explanation lists organic clues as onset after age 35, lack of anticipatory anxiety, lack of avoidance behaviour, no personal or family history of anxiety disorders, and poor response to short-term anxiolytics - so avoidance, family history, significant anticipatory anxiety and onset before 25 are the options that argue **AGAINST** an organic cause.

Lactate infusion: nearly ==72%== of patients with panic disorder have a panic attack when given **IV** sodium lactate, so lactate provocation is used to confirm a diagnosis of panic disorder. Hyperventilation and **CO2** inhalation have been used. Panic attacks triggered by sodium lactate are not inhibited by peripherally acting beta-blockers but are inhibited by benzodiazepines and tricyclic drugs.

**EMI** biochemical matches: panic disorder = **LACTATE** provocation (nearly ==72%== have a panic attack on **IV** sodium lactate); differentiating pseudoseizures from true epileptic attacks = **SERUM** **PROLACTIN** (elevated within 15-20 minutes of a true seizure, not in pseudoseizures); neuroleptic malignant syndrome = serum **CREATININE** **PHOSPHOKINASE** (raised); **SIADH** induced by antidepressants = **URINE** **ANALYSIS** (urine osmolality high despite hyponatraemia); depression = **DEXAMETHASONE** suppression test (failure of feedback suppression of cortisol).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/EMIS all chapters/EMIs Clinical Examination.pdf

blocks.text: Narcoanalysis: interviews with amobarbital are very rarely used in current clinical practice. They are sometimes helpful in differentiating nonorganic from organic conditions, particularly in catatonia, stupor and muteness. Organic conditions tend to worsen with amobarbital infusions, but nonorganic or psychogenic conditions tend to get better because of disinhibition, decreased anxiety or increased relaxation. Therapeutically, amobarbital interviews are useful in disorders of repression and dissociation such as amnesia and fugue. Benzodiazepines can be substituted for amobarbital.

The **NOT**-true narcoanalysis statement is that **ORGANIC** muteness gets better with amobarbital infusion: organic conditions tend to worsen with amobarbital, whereas non-organic (psychogenic) conditions improve, which is how it helps separate catatonia, stupor and muteness; it is useful when repression and dissociation are suspected, and benzodiazepines can be used.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

bullets.text: Medical causes of panic: paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, PE, seizures, Meniere's, TIA, carcinoid, Cushing's, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycaemia, phaeochromocytoma.
Examine all first presentations; extensive medical work-up only if features suggest physical disease.
Sodium lactate triggers panic in about 72% of panic disorder patients; blocked by benzodiazepines and tricyclics, not peripherally acting beta-blockers.
Amobarbital: organic muteness/stupor/catatonia worsens, psychogenic improves; therapeutic in repression and dissociation (amnesia, fugue); benzodiazepines can substitute.

sections.title: 8. Laboratory assessment: psychosis

blocks.text: Differential diagnoses to consider in the history of presenting illness: head trauma (subdural haematoma), seizures, new-onset headaches, focal neurological deficits, abnormal body movements, memory loss, and tremor especially in older patients, recreational drug use, and dietary history (deficiencies of vitamin **B12**, folate, **thiamine** and niacin can all cause psychosis).

Chronic **SUBDURAL** haematoma, not subarachnoid haemorrhage, fits a middle-aged man with headache, poor concentration, fluctuating memory loss, unequal pupils and mild papilloedema: subarachnoid haemorrhage presents more acutely with raised intracranial tension signs and focal deficits, whereas chronic subdural haematoma is commonly seen in the elderly and alcoholics, usually after a mild head injury, with about 4-5 weeks between the trauma and diagnosis and an insidious presentation.
Physical examination: vital signs, level of consciousness, evidence of malnutrition, signs of hypo- or hyperthyroidism or cushingoid features, and rashes associated with autoimmune disorders,
and dysmorphic facial features (genetic syndromes e.g. velocardiofacial), focal neurological signs and examination for signs of raised intracranial pressure.

blocks.caption: Table image: Initial tests in psychosis (TESTS | WHY DO WE DO IT?) - full blood count, thyroid profile, blood glucose/lipid profile/ECG, prolactin levels, electrolytes, GFR and creatinine, liver function tests, blood and urine toxicology screen.

blocks.text: Memory loss and personality change with **WING-BEATING** tremor is Wilson's disease, so the biochemical abnormality to identify is **LOW** **SERUM** **CERULOPLASMIN** (copper deposits in the lenticular nuclei) - not low albumin, calcium, thyroxine or serotonin.

Porphyrias: acute intermittent porphyria (**AIP**) is one of the groups of disorders of haem metabolism, characterised by neurological and psychiatric manifestations without obvious cutaneous markers.

**AIP** manifests with abdominal pain, neuropathies and constipation, but unlike most types of porphyria patients do not have a rash. It is autosomal dominant with presentation starting between ages 18 and 40. It is episodic, and episodes are often triggered by certain medications including estrogens, barbiturates and benzodiazepines; diclofenac can precipitate an episode. Psychiatric manifestations include depression, anxiety, delirium and psychosis. The most important lab test is demonstrating increased urinary porphobilinogen during acute attacks. Treatment is aimed at reducing haem synthesis by administering haemin.

Constipation and acute abdominal pain, leg weakness after hypnotics and diclofenac, with visual and tactile hallucinations and intense anxiety = **ACUTE** **INTERMITTENT** **PORPHYRIA**: the test is **URINE** **PORPHYRINS** (not serum folate, lipids, ceruloplasmin or urine glucose); **AIP** shows neurological and psychiatric manifestations without obvious cutaneous markers.

sections.title: 9. Autoimmune encephalitis presenting as psychosis (anti-NMDAR)

blocks.text: Autoimmune disorders with antibodies against crucial neurotransmitter receptors can present with psychosis. The receptors most vulnerable (anecdotal reports) are: voltage-gated potassium channel complex (**LGI1**, **CASPR2**, contactin-2), **NMDA** receptor, **AMPA** receptor, **GABA-B** and glycine receptor.

Some studies estimate that ==6.3%== of first-onset psychosis patients have pathogenic antibodies against brain receptors (Zandi et al., 2011). The best known syndrome is anti-**NMDA** receptor (**NMDAR**) encephalitis.

blocks.title: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis: key features
rows: Anti-**NMDAR** antibodies cause titre-dependent destruction of synaptic **NMDAR** through crosslinking and internalisation
Around ==4%== of patients with anti-**NMDAR** present with isolated psychiatric symptoms
More common in females (==80%==) than males
About ==50%== of women with anti-**NMDAR** have an underlying ovarian teratoma
==75%== of patients first present to a psychiatrist with acute psychosis and/or mania
Psychosis usually presents with a prodromal illness (fever, headaches, malaise)

blocks.text: Investigations in suspected cases: serum **NMDAR** and **VGKC** antibodies; **ANA**, **CRP**, **ESR**, **FBC**, U+E (low sodium is seen in those with anti-**VGKC** antibodies); if strong suspicion, **EEG** (encephalopathy with disorganised delta/theta activity) and **MRI** brain.

**MRI** brain looks for medial temporal hyperintensity, usually on **T2** or **FLAIR** sequences, in the hippocampi, frontobasal and insular regions and basal ganglia; it is normal in about ==50%==. Confirmatory diagnosis requires **CSF** analysis: lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein and oligoclonal bands in about ==60%== of cases; almost all have intrathecal anti-**NMDAR** antibodies.

Patients cured of anti-**NMDAR** encephalitis may continue having detectable antibodies in serum and/or **CSF**; **CSF** antibodies rise during each relapse. Elevated creatine kinase is a non-specific feature. In females, ask for ultrasound or **CT** pelvis.

Anti-**NMDAR** encephalitis usually responds to 3 days of methylprednisolone (oral or **IV**) followed by oral prednisolone, with 5 days of plasma exchange. Remission can be maintained by (1) steroids alone; (2) steroids with a steroid-sparing agent such as azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil; or (3) rituximab.

Regular benzodiazepines may be required. **AVOID** **ANTIPSYCHOTICS**: dystonic reactions and **NMS**-like syndrome with rigidity, hyperthermia and autonomic instability might occur on their use in patients with anti-**NMDAR** antibodies.

blocks.note: Not in the notes (they cover autoimmune encephalitis): lymphocytic pleocytosis with many red cells in the **CSF**, hyperintensity of the left temporal lobe on **T2**-weighted **MRI** and lateralised periodic discharges on **EEG** in a semi-conscious patient point to herpes encephalitis (keyed over pneumococcal meningitis, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, temporal lobe malignancy and subdural haemorrhage); the explanation adds that early **MRI** may be negative, which does not rule out **HSV** encephalitis, and that **T2** hyperintensity favours the medial temporal lobes.

bullets.text: Receptors targeted by autoimmune psychosis: VGKC complex, NMDA, AMPA, GABA-B, glycine.

sections.title: 11. Anorexia nervosa: investigations and BMI

blocks.title: Expected abnormalities in anorexia (adapted from Fairburn & Harrison, 2003)
rows: Low **LH**, **FSH** and oestradiol; low **T3**, **T4** in low normal range, normal **TSH** (low **T3** syndrome); mild increase in plasma cortisol; raised growth hormone; severe hypoglycaemia (rare); low leptin (but possibly higher than expected for bodyweight)
**ECG** abnormalities (especially with electrolyte disturbance): conduction defects, especially prolongation of the Q-T interval, of major concern
Delayed gastric emptying; decreased colonic motility (secondary to chronic laxative misuse); acute gastric dilatation (rare, secondary to binge eating or excessive re-feeding)
Moderate normocytic normochromic anaemia; mild leucopenia with relative lymphocytosis; thrombocytopenia
Hypercholesterolaemia; raised serum carotene; hypophosphataemia (exaggerated during refeeding); dehydration; electrolyte disturbance

blocks.text: Electrolyte disturbance is varied in form and present in those who frequently vomit or misuse large quantities of laxatives or diuretics. Vomiting results in metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia (loss of hydrochloric acid from gastric juices). Laxative misuse results in metabolic acidosis, hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia.

During laxative-induced diarrhoea a large amount of bicarbonate may be lost in the stool; with normal kidneys it is replaced and no serious base deficit develops, but with poor renal blood flow due to hypovolaemia/starvation, base deficit and acidosis develop rapidly. Acidosis also results from excessive lactic acid production in severe diarrhoea.
Other abnormalities: osteopenia and osteoporosis (heightened fracture risk); enlarged cerebral ventricles and external **CSF** spaces (pseudo atrophy).

Repeated **VOMITING** in anorexia gives hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic **ALKALOSIS** (loss of gastric acid); metabolic **ACIDOSIS** results from **LAXATIVE** abuse - metabolic acidosis, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia are the tempting options.

sections.title: 12. Alcohol use disorders: tests and complications

blocks.text: No single lab test can dependably diagnose alcohol abuse. Of available tests (**GGT**, mean corpuscular volume, breathalyzer, carbohydrate deficient transferrin - **CDT**), the **CDT** is the single most specific and sensitive test for detecting heavy alcohol use over the last 10 days. Because of high intersubject variability it is best to compare **CDT** with the patient's own baseline. In primary care, **AUDIT** is often considered the best screening tool.

blocks.title: Systemic complications of alcohol abuse
rows: Seizures (intoxication or withdrawal), Wernicke's encephalopathy, Korsakoff's dementia, polyneuropathy, coma, amnesia, alcoholic dementia, cerebellar degeneration, damage to corpus callosum (Marchiafava syndrome)
**GI** bleeds, peptic ulcer, malnutrition (especially **thiamine**), Mallory-Weiss tears, oesophageal strictures, fatty liver, hepatic cirrhosis, portal hypertension, pancreatitis and hypoglycaemia
Pancytopenia, folic acid and **B12** deficiency resulting in **MCV** changes and anaemia, clotting disorders due to liver failure, immune compromise
Lung cancer, pneumonia due to aspiration under intoxication
Renal failure, hepatorenal syndrome, hyponatraemia and other electrolyte imbalances
Testicular atrophy, sexual disorders, menstrual irregularities
Low birth weight, foetal alcohol syndrome, developmental delays, neural tube defects due to maternal malnourishment

blocks.text: **EMI** alcohol-test matches: **GGT** = the **SENSITIVE** marker (levels normalise 2-4 weeks after abstinence); carbohydrate-deficient transferrin = accurately predicts **RECENT** alcohol abuse and detects relapse; mean corpuscular volume = the more **SPECIFIC** test, less useful for relapse; **AUDIT** = best screening tool in primary care. Note the notes call **CDT** the single most specific and sensitive test for heavy drinking over the last 10 days - match on the question's own wording.

sections.title: 13. Specific investigations: ECG/QTc and urine drug testing

blocks.text: The major use of **ECG** in a psychiatric ward, apart from emergencies, is to measure **QT** interval when treating patients with antipsychotics. Prolonged **QT** can predispose to fatal ventricular arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes (polymorphic ventricular tachycardia).

QTc is **QT** corrected for heart rate. It is valuable for classifying risk groups but not a precise predictor of torsades (low positive predictive value). Different methods to derive QTc from **QT** give markedly different values. Risk is said to increase if QTc is beyond normal limits (440 ms for men; 470 ms for women); anything more than 500 ms is clearly an increased risk. **QT** varies with gender, time of day, food intake, alcohol intake, menstrual cycle and **ECG** lead used.

Risk factors for prolonged QTc: congenital long **QT** syndrome; underlying heart disease, bradycardia, heart failure and ischaemic disease; female gender; extremes of age; liver disease; electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia); illicit drug use (principally stimulants); starvation or anorexia; high physical exertion (agitation); high dosages of the drug lengthening **QT**; rapid infusion of torsadogenic drugs.

Urine drug testing is one of the most frequently used lab investigations in psychiatry. When a patient repeatedly gives negative urine samples despite strong suspicion, a cheap and quick check is the specific gravity, which reveals adulteration of urine with tap water.

blocks.title: Time substances remain present in urine
rows: Occasional use - up to 3 days. High daily use for long time - up to 4 weeks.

bullets.text: ECG on psychiatric wards mainly measures QT when using antipsychotics; prolonged QT risks torsades de pointes.

Urine detection: alcohol up to 12 h, amphetamine up to 48 h, benzodiazepine 3 days, cocaine 6-8 h (metabolites 2-4 days), heroin 1-3 days, morphine 2-3 days, codeine 48 h, methadone 3+ days, PCP 8 days.
Cannabis in urine: up to 3 days occasional use; up to 4 weeks high daily long-term use.

sections.title: 14. Renal disturbances, SIADH, polydipsia and diabetes insipidus

blocks.text: Renal disease in cocaine and heroin abusers has been associated with nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis, amyloidosis, interstitial nephritis and rhabdomyolysis. In a heroin user with a puffy face, hypertension and weight gain, suspect heroin-related nephropathy. Infective endocarditis, **HIV**, and **HBV** and **HCV** infections are associated with renal pathologic patterns similar to those the drug itself can cause. In Black patients focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is often seen, while in Whites mostly membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

Urine analysis may be important for **SIADH** induced by antidepressants or antipsychotics, psychogenic polydipsia (excessive water consumption without obvious organic illness) and diabetes insipidus due to **lithium** (nephrogenic) or head injury (central).

blocks.text: A puffy face, weight gain despite normal appetite and **BP** 150/100 in a young African-American intravenous heroin user = **NEPHROPATHY** ('heroin-associated nephropathy' = focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, with proteinuria that may be nephrotic range, more common among Black heroin users) - not hypothyroidism, opiate withdrawal, hepatitis B or **HIV** seroconversion.

blocks.text: A diabetic on antidepressants with polyuria and polydipsia and **BOTH** urine and plasma osmolality low = **PSYCHOGENIC** **POLYDIPSIA** (water overload; excessive fluid intake without an organic cause), not diabetes insipidus, **SIADH**, hyponatraemia or hyperglycaemia - the explanation says a high-normal plasma value with urine osmolality below plasma points the other way, to diabetes insipidus.

blocks.text: Polydipsia and polyuria are not features of **SIADH** or hyponatraemia per se. The clinical features of **SIADH** are attributed to water retention, hyponatraemia and hypo-osmolality of the serum.

Most hyponatraemic patients have no symptoms or signs until serum sodium falls below 125 mmol/L. Initially: lethargy, muscle cramps, anorexia, nausea, vomiting. More rapid or profound hyponatraemia: coma, convulsions, death. Longer term: altered consciousness, headache, impaired memory, confusion. If serum sodium drops below 110-115 mmol/L, seizures and irreversible brain damage can occur.

blocks.text: Acute hyperventilation (often in a panic attack in a psychiatric clinic) may present with agitation, increased breathing rate with shallow breaths (tachypnoea), chest pain, dizziness, palpitations, tetanic cramps (carpopedal spasm), paraesthesias, generalised weakness and syncope. Paraesthesias are due to acid-base imbalance, occur more commonly in the upper extremity and are usually bilateral; unilateral paraesthesias are left-sided in approximately ==80%== of cases. Perioral numbness is very common.

Hyperventilation (often in a panic attack) causes **PARAESTHESIA** - not nystagmus, hyper-reflexia, vertigo or ataxia: usually in the upper extremity and bilateral (unilateral ones are left-sided in about ==80%==), with perioral numbness very common; the explanation also lists agitation, tachypnoea, chest pain, carpopedal spasm, weakness and syncope.

Minor Physical Anomalies (MPAs) are often observed in a range of developmental disorders. MPAs are also more frequent in patients and siblings of patients with schizophrenia than in healthy controls, supporting a neurodevelopmental aetiology. MPAs can be rated using the Lane Scale.

blocks.caption: Boxed list image: Minor Physical Anomalies in putative developmental disorders (preauricular tag through Brushfield spots), including the printed note on simian crease.

blocks.text: MPAs in putative developmental disorders: preauricular tag, preauricular pits, lip pit, bifid uvula, supernumerary nipples, partial syndactyly (generally toes 2-3), pigmented naevi, cafe-au-lait spots, sacral haemangioma, prominent or flat occiput, prominent or flat forehead, primitive shape of ears, earlobe crease, fine electric hair, tongue with smooth and rough spots, double antihelix, simian crease, single flexion crease on 5th finger, sole crease, prominent heel, double posterior hair whorl, multiple buccal frenula, furrowed tongue, Brushfield spots.

A simian crease is a single uninterrupted palmar crease traversing the palm from the radial to the ulnar border instead of the two usual creases; to be considered an anomaly the line should be uninterrupted.

blocks.note: Not in the notes (they list constricted pupils under opiate intoxication): tolerance develops to the miotic effect of mu-opioid agonists, so patients on large long-term doses do not have miotic pupils unless measured in bright light, and dark pupillography can be used to study opioid dependence - the question keys opioids as the dependence revealed when an eye-drop test fails to dilate the pupils.

Not in the notes beyond hepatic complications of alcohol: episodic irritability, altered sleep-wake cycle, personality change, poor memory, palmar erythema, subcutaneous bleeds and bilateral plantar extensor reflexes point to hepatic failure - which can produce asterixis, tremors, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes and altered consciousness after a history of personality change, abrupt mood swings and cognitive deterioration; peripheral signs include subcutaneous bleeds, pedal oedema, ascites and palmar erythema.

Not in the notes (they list dilated pupils under stimulant abuse): high blood pressure, rapid pulse, warm moist skin, pressured speech, fine tremor and hyperreflexia point to a stimulant; stimulants induce alertness, euphoria, insomnia and anorexia, may cause psychotic symptoms, and raise blood pressure and heart rate.

Not in the notes (myasthenia gravis appears only under dysarthria): a man with severe depression, bilateral ptosis and reduced muscle tone most likely has myasthenia gravis - weakness that varies over minutes or days and fatigability (worse with repeated use, better with rest); 15-==20%== of people diagnosed with myasthenia develop depression.

Not in the notes beyond minor physical anomalies supporting a neurodevelopmental aetiology: the statement that does **NOT** support the neurodevelopmental hypothesis is an excess of **PROGRESSIVE** structural brain abnormalities - patients exhibit non-progressive abnormalities (more cranio-facial and dermatoglyphic minor physical anomalies, lower average **IQ**, subtle psychomotor, behavioural and social abnormalities), and progressive change would imply an ongoing disease process.

blocks.text: The vestibular portion transmits information about linear and angular accelerations of the head from the utricle, saccule and semicircular canals to the vestibular nucleus. The Romberg test evaluates vestibular control of balance: standing with feet together and eyes closed, the patient tends to fall toward the side of vestibular hypofunction. Romberg may also be positive in polyneuropathies and dorsal column disease, but these patients do not fall consistently to one side.
Caloric testing: normally on cold water testing nystagmus is noted to the opposite side; warm water elicits nystagmus towards the same side.

blocks.note: Not in the notes: bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia is the eye sign pathognomonic of multiple sclerosis (in young patients it is often the underlying cause; in older patients with one-sided ophthalmoplegia stroke is more common); it arises from dysfunction of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, with impaired adduction and abducting nystagmus on conjugate gaze, causing horizontal diplopia.

Not in the notes: left occipital lobe damage after a stroke produces cortical blindness - total or partial loss of vision in a normal-appearing eye from occipital cortex damage, most often from unilateral or bilateral posterior cerebral artery blockage; some vision may recover.

Not in the notes: a parietal lobe vascular lesion produces a lower homonymous quadrantanopia (damage to the optic radiation as it passes through the parietal lobes) - keyed over bitemporal hemianopia, homonymous hemianopia, one-sided blindness and upper quadrantanopia.

Not in the notes (**EMI**): keyhole vision after a major stroke = cortical blindness (usually posterior cerebral artery occlusion; in effect a bilateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing); sudden blindness with patchy spirals of field loss = tunnel vision (seen in hysteria or malingering; conversion disorder); the field larger at 2 m than at 1 m = funnel vision (glaucoma among organic causes); a blind patient who denies the defect = Anton's syndrome; one-quarter of the field affected on one side = quadrantanopia.

bullets.text: Cranial nerves I-XII with bedside tests: smell, acuity/fields/pupils, eye movements, facial and corneal sensation, facial movement, balance/hearing, palate/cough, shrug, tongue.

CN VIII: vestibular - Romberg/caloric; cochlear - Rinne and Weber.

Rinne: in conductive loss bone conduction exceeds air conduction; in sensorineural loss both are reduced similarly.
Romberg: patient falls to the side of vestibular hypofunction; also positive in polyneuropathy and dorsal column disease but without consistent side.
Caloric mnemonic COWS: cold - opposite, warm - same.

sections.title: 17. Neurological soft signs and cerebellar signs

blocks.text: Neurological signs are often referred to as 'hard' or 'soft'. Hard signs are impairments of basic motor and sensory functions that are localisable to the pyramidal, extrapyramidal or cranial nerve systems.

Soft signs are non-localisable neurological findings thought to reflect neurodevelopmental aberrations when seen in psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, autism, **OCD** and **ADHD**. The hard/soft distinction is artificial, reflecting inability to define the brain-behaviour relationship underlying certain neurological abnormalities.

Three groups of symptoms are collectively known as soft signs: abnormalities of motor coordination, sensory integration, and signs of cortical disinhibition. Neuroimaging studies implicating several parts of the brain in soft signs further blur their distinction from hard signs.

blocks.caption: Boxed list image: Common soft neurological signs in psychosis (choreoathetosis through frontal release).

blocks.text: Common soft neurological signs in psychosis: choreoathetosis (predating psychosis, especially in children), abnormal gait, grimacing, abnormal reflexes, changes in muscle tone, abnormal saccades, frequent blinking, dysdiadochokinesia, astereognosis, poor left-right discrimination, anosognosia, apraxia, gaze impersistence, frontal release.

The cerebellum provides an important feedback loop for coordination of muscle activity. Midline cerebellar dysfunction results in ataxia of gait, difficulty maintaining upright posture and truncal ataxia. The lateral cerebellar hemispheres (neocerebellum) control movement of the ipsilateral limbs; the midline vermis controls truncal tone, speech and eye movements; the flocculonodular lobe (archicerebellum) is involved in vestibular functions.

blocks.title: Cerebellar signs (part 1)
rows: Difficulties in coordinating truncal and limb movements, often seen in midline damage. Tested using tandem walking (heel-to-toe walk).
Reduced muscle tone resulting in loss of 'checking' effect when passively manipulated (leg swinging test results in pendular swinging of legs until passive inertia sets in)
An oscillating tremor that accelerates in pace on approaching the target
Loss of smoothness of execution of a motor activity
Overshooting or undershooting of a target while attempting to reach an object

blocks.title: Cerebellar signs (part 2)
rows: Inability to perform rapid alternating movements. Tested by asking the patient to tap one hand on the other repeatedly while simultaneously pronating and supinating the hand.
Inability to tap and keep a rhythm
Staccato or scanning speech with poor modulation of volume and pitch; usually a sign of diffuse involvement of the cerebellum

bullets.text: Hard signs are localisable motor/sensory deficits; soft signs are non-localisable, thought to reflect neurodevelopmental aberration (schizophrenia, autism, OCD, ADHD).
Soft signs group into motor coordination, sensory integration and cortical disinhibition abnormalities; the hard/soft distinction is artificial.
Cerebellar anatomy: lateral hemispheres - ipsilateral limbs; vermis - truncal tone, speech, eye movements; flocculonodular lobe - vestibular.
Cerebellar signs: ataxia, hypotonia, intention tremor, dyssynergia, dysmetria (past pointing).
More cerebellar signs: dysdiadochokinesis, dysrhythmia, dysarthria (staccato/scanning speech, diffuse involvement).
Finger-nose or heel-shin tests elicit dyssynergia, dysmetria and tremor.

blocks.text: Meningeal signs can be elicited in the presence of meningeal inflammation or irritation due to haemorrhage/trauma.

blocks.text: Cortical sensory signs: the cortical sensory system includes the somatosensory cortex and its central connections. Functions include kinaesthetic sensation, stereognosis, graphaesthesia, tactile localisation and tactile 2-point discrimination on both sides of the body. Position sensation is tested with the subject's eyes closed, by passively moving distal joints in various directions.
Fibrillations are not visible to the naked eye except when the tongue is affected.

Spasms with a slow writhing character along the long axis of the limbs or body; the patient may assume peculiar postures

Fasciculations usually benign but if widespread may indicate neuromuscular disease such as ALS.

sections.title: 19. Reflexes, neurocutaneous signs and speech abnormalities

blocks.text: Primitive reflexes include the glabellar tap, rooting, snout, sucking and palmomental reflexes. They are generally absent in adults; when present they signify diffuse cerebral damage, particularly of the frontal lobes (hence 'frontal-release signs').

Superficial reflexes are segmental reflex responses indicating the integrity of cutaneous innervation and the corresponding motor outflow: corneal, conjunctival, abdominal, cremasteric and plantar (Babinski) reflexes.

The **CREMASTERIC** reflex is the option that is **NOT** a frontal release sign (rooting, glabellar tap, snout and grasp are): primitive reflexes, generally absent in adults, signify diffuse cerebral damage - particularly of the frontal lobes - when present, whereas the cremasteric reflex is a superficial reflex.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Corneal and conjunctival reflexes: afferent via the 5th nerve, efferent via the 7th nerve. Abdominal reflex: drawing a line away from the umbilicus along the diagonals of the 4 abdominal quadrants; a normal reflex draws the umbilicus toward the line. Cremasteric reflex: scratching the medial thigh elicits scrotal contraction, normally elevating the ipsilateral testis.

Plantar (Babinski) reflex: the normal response is plantar flexion of the great toe (absent/negative Babinski). Dorsiflexion of the great toe (positive Babinski) suggests an upper motor neuron lesion. Lack of either response may indicate absent cutaneous innervation in the **S1** segment or loss of motor innervation in the **L5** segment ipsilaterally.

Deep tendon reflexes require intact cutaneous innervation, motor supply and cortical input to the spinal segment. They are exaggerated in **UMN** lesions and absent in respective **LMN** lesions. Pseudobulbar palsy is a **UMN** lesion with exaggerated jaw jerk; bulbar palsy is an **LMN** lesion with absent jaw jerk.

bullets.text: Primitive reflexes (glabellar, rooting, snout, sucking, palmomental) are absent in adults; their presence signals diffuse frontal damage (frontal-release signs).
Superficial reflexes: corneal, conjunctival, abdominal, cremasteric, plantar; corneal afferent via CN V, efferent via CN VII.
Positive Babinski (great toe dorsiflexion) suggests UMN lesion; normal is plantar flexion.
Deep tendon reflexes: exaggerated in UMN lesions, absent in LMN lesions; roots: biceps C5-6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, patellar L2-4, Achilles S4.

Neurocutaneous: ash leaf macules and ungual fibromas - tuberous sclerosis; cafe au lait spots - neurofibromata/tuberous sclerosis; axillary freckling - neurofibroma; frontal baldness - myotonic dystrophy.
Dysarthria: spastic (bilateral UMN), flaccid (LMN), ataxic (scanning, cerebellar), hypokinetic (breathy monotone), hyperkinetic (basal ganglia), mixed.
Hysterical aphonia: sudden voice loss with normal examination and preserved vocal cord activity.

sections.title: 20. Gait

blocks.text: Gait is the motor attitude of a person in the upright position.

blocks.title: Gait patterns described
rows: Stroke affecting the pyramidal system. Typically clenched hand with extended knee and plantarflexed ankle; the paralysed leg appears longer (pole-like) so the patient circles it, giving repeated circumduction of the affected leg.
Mild cases elicited only by tandem walking; severe cases show a staggering wide-based gait. Unilateral cerebellar lesions may cause veering to the side of the lesion (sailor's gait).
Parkinsonian patients: very short steps, shuffles legs rather than propelling them forward; progressively short steps from a tendency to accelerate (festinating gait).
High steps as if climbing stairs on a level surface; seen in chronic peripheral neuropathies (e.g. drop foot) and dorsal column disorders.

Proximal myopathy: broad-based, duck-like waddle from dropping of the pelvis to the side of the raised leg, with compensatory forward lumbar curvature; also congenital hip dislocation and near-term pregnancy.

Spastic paraplegia: marked rigidity and excessive adduction of the swinging leg with plantar flexion of the ankle and knee flexion due to contractures, giving forced tip-toe walking with knees rubbing together and crossing like scissors.

sections.title: 23. Bedside cognitive examination tools

blocks.text: **MMSE**: the standard screening instrument for dementia, introduced by Folstein in 1976. It takes 5-10 minutes and has a median positive likelihood ratio of 6.3 and median negative likelihood ratio of 0.19.

**MMSE** properties: brief tool for grading cognitive impairment in the elderly and screening for dementia; not very sensitive to change but used in anti-dementia drug trials (**ADAS**-Cog may be better at detecting change); practice effect may occur; 30-point scale; with less than 9 years of formal education the cut-off for suspecting dementia is 21/22 rather than the usual 23/24; insensitive to early decline; does not pick up frontal executive defects.

blocks.caption: Table image: ITEMS in MMSE - Orientation (10); Registration (3) and recall (3) tasks (6 points total); Attention task (5); Multistep command (3); Naming (2); Repetition language (1); Reading comprehension (close your eyes, 1 point); Writing (1); Visual construction (copy interlocking polygons, 1 point).

blocks.text: Clinical interview with carers and patients is the best diagnostic tool for any disorder including dementia; overreliance on **MMSE** scores can be counterproductive.

The single most useful tool for **DIAGNOSING** dementia is the clinical interview of the patient **AND** the carer - not **MMSE**, **MRI**, neuropsychological testing or **CT**: nothing can replace a careful clinical interview for diagnostic evaluation of most disorders.

Clock drawing test: requires verbal understanding (comprehension), short-term working memory to process the instruction, and spatially coded knowledge in addition to constructive skills and planning (executive function). It does not test orientation to time.

**ORIENTATION** **TO** **TIME** is the domain **NOT** needed for the clock-drawing test (executive function, constructional praxis, comprehension and visuospatial ability are): the explanation states the clock-drawing test does not assess orientation to time.

blocks.text: Watson's 7-score screening method: three digits in a quadrant is correct; an error score of 1 is assigned to each of the first three quadrants containing errors and 4 to the fourth quadrant, maximum 7. Normal range 0-3. A score of 4 or more has sensitivity ==87%==, specificity ==82%== and kappa 0.70 for identifying dementia (**NINCDS-ADRDA** probable dementia).

Clock drawing correlates highly with the **MMSE** and other cognitive tests, and can diagnose unilateral neglect and inattention. Subjects of low education, advanced age and depression perform more poorly. Normal clock-drawing ability reasonably excludes cognitive impairment.

Addenbrooke's cognitive examination (**ACE-R**) evaluates six cognitive domains (orientation, attention, memory, verbal fluency, language and visuospatial ability); useful for detecting dementia and mild cognitive impairment.

**ACE** includes frontal tests such as verbal fluency, making it more sensitive to frontal types of dementia than the **MMSE** (Hodges et al., 2000); it also differentiates dementia subtypes (Alzheimer's, frontotemporal dementia, progressive supranuclear palsy and other parkinsonism-associated dementias). **ACE-R** cut-offs: <88 (sensitivity 0.94, specificity 0.89) and <82 (sensitivity 0.84, specificity 1.0); likelihood ratio for a positive test at 82 is 100:1. The language domain receives the major share of the scoring.

For **GLOBAL** cognitive functioning the keyed instrument is the **ADDENBROOKE**'S cognitive examination (not Mini-Cog, clock drawing, **MMSE** or Montreal cognitive assessment): it tests orientation, attention, memory, verbal fluency, language and visuospatial ability, incorporating the **MMSE** questions and expanding memory, language and visuospatial concepts while adding verbal fluency.

For the **ACE-R**, a score below 82 gives a high **SPECIFICITY** for dementia (1.0, with sensitivity 0.84; likelihood ratio 100:1), whereas below 88 gives sensitivity 0.94 and specificity 0.89 - do not swap sensitivity and specificity; the language domain (not visuospatial) carries the major share of the score and frontal tests such as verbal fluency are included.

sections.title: 24. Imaging of the nervous system: CT and MRI

blocks.text: **CT** is the most widely available scan in clinical practice. Scanners take a series of head X-ray pictures from 360 degrees around the head; image contrast reflects the degree to which tissues absorb X-rays. Structures close to bone (e.g. brainstem) may appear obscured; the difference in attenuation between grey and white matter is not very high; **CT** is limited to one plane of rotation, often axial.

Tumours and inflammation can be appreciated with **IV** iodine-containing contrast, which absorbs much more radiation than brain tissue and so appears bright. Calcification, which may be invisible in **MRI**, is better visualised on **CT**.

**MRI** does not rely on X-ray absorption but on the nuclear magnetic resonance principle; magnets are rated in Tesla (T). Odd-numbered nuclei (**H1** in particular) align with the magnetic field; after a radiofrequency pulse at 90 or 180 degrees they realign and emit their own radiofrequency signal, which scanners collect. Images can be axial, coronal or sagittal. Hydrogen nuclei within fat realign rapidly and within water slowly. Routine **MRI** uses **T1** and **T2** pulse sequences.

sections.title: 25. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy and functional MRI

blocks.text: **MR** spectroscopy can detect several biologically important nuclei with an odd number of protons and neutrons.

H-1 proton spectroscopy can quantify N-acetyl aspartate (**NAA**), creatine and choline-containing molecules. **GABA** and glutamate can be detected using **MRS** but not dopamine, as it is available in a very low concentration.

Phosphorus-31 **MRS** can be used to determine the pH of brain regions and the concentrations of phosphorus-containing compounds (e.g. **ATP** and **GTP**) that are important in the metabolic activity of the brain.

blocks.text: **MRS** can also measure concentrations of psychotherapeutic drugs such as **lithium** in the brain. Some compounds, such as **fluoxetine** and **trifluoperazine** (Stelazine), contain fluorine-19, which can also be detected in the brain and measured by **MRS**.

fMRI: neuronal activity causes a local increase in oxygen consumption, so local deoxyhaemoglobin rises relative to oxyhaemoglobin. Oxyhaemoglobin is diamagnetic (weak magnetic contrast) while deoxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic, producing an **MR** signal detectable with the **T2** sequence. This is the Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (**BOLD**) technique, the basis for functional **MRI**.

fMRI is a proxy measure of tissue activity that depends on relative changes in perfusion; it does not measure actual neuronal metabolism. No radioactive isotopes are administered, a significant advantage over **PET** and **SPECT**. A subject can perform experimental and control tasks in the same session.

In resting fMRI, regions with high activity at rest (precuneus, lateral parietal regions and medial prefrontal cortex) are studied; a network of these regions with higher baseline activity at rest is the default mode network (**DMN**).

sections.title: 26. SPECT, PET and diffusion tensor imaging

blocks.text: **SPECT** uses radioactive compounds to study regional differences in cerebral blood flow, recording the pattern of photon emission from the bloodstream, which varies with perfusion. Like fMRI it does not measure neuronal metabolism directly. It uses compounds labelled with single photon-emitting isotopes: iodine-123, technetium-99m and xenon-133.

Xenon-133 quickly enters the blood and distributes as a function of regional blood flow (the regional cerebral blood flow, rCBF, technique); it measures blood flow only on the surface of the brain, an important limitation.

Whole-brain blood flow with **SPECT** requires injectable tracers such as technetium-99m-d,l-hexamethyl propylene amine oxime (**HMPAO**), attached to highly lipophilic molecules that cross the blood-brain barrier and are enzymatically converted to charged ions that remain trapped in the cell, concentrating in areas of relatively higher blood flow. This is the ligand most commonly used to detect perfusion changes in dementia.

**PET** can study blood flow, receptor distribution and metabolic activity of brain tissue. In **SPECT** a single particle is emitted, whereas in **PET** two particles are emitted; the latter reaction gives a more precise location and better resolution. **PET** isotopes decay by emitting positrons, with resolution closer to its theoretical minimum of 3 mm.

Relatively few **PET** scanners are available because an on-site cyclotron is needed to make the isotopes. The most commonly used isotopes are fluorine-18, nitrogen-13 and oxygen-15, usually linked to another molecule except oxygen-15. The most commonly employed ligand is [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose (**FDG**), which gives direct information about neuronal metabolism.

blocks.text: Diffusion tensor imaging (**DTI**) combines nuclear magnetic resonance and molecular diffusion (random Brownian motion). The predominant direction of molecular movement helps determine the integrity and trace white matter tracts. Traditional diffusion weighted images apply only 3 gradient directions; **DTI** allows multiple (e.g. 16).

From **DTI**, measures such as Fractional Anisotropy (**FA**), an index of white matter integrity, can be calculated; the principal direction of the diffusion tensor is used in tractography to infer white-matter connectivity.

bullets.text: Depression: periventricular/deep WM and thalamic/striatal hyperintensities; reduced frontal and basal ganglia volumes; lower prefrontal, cingulate, amygdala metabolism.
Depression: higher anterior cingulate/prefrontal metabolism predicts better treatment response; higher 5HT2A density, raised MAO-A, raised D2 binding (psychomotor retardation).
Therapeutic SSRI dose occupies 80% of 5HT transporters.
Schizophrenia: ventricular enlargement; grey matter loss (insula, anterior cingulate, medial temporal); progressive volume loss in first years; poor DLPFC activation; low NAA in PFC; reduced FA.
Alzheimer's: ventricular enlargement, loss of temporal volume especially hippocampus, reduced parieto-temporal fMRI activation and SPECT flow.
OCD: caudate volumes reduced and increased reported; higher caudate blood flow that falls with effective treatment.

blocks.subtopic: Complex figure copying: right versus left hemisphere
blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q27** - with right hemisphere damage patients reproduce the details but miss the Gestalt (global features); with left hemisphere damage they reproduce the global features but make inaccurate internal details, so a patient who manages the global features but misses the finer details most likely has left hemisphere damage.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q11** - a previously reliable man who becomes irritable, profane and irresponsible over months most likely has a frontal lobe tumour (frontal lobe syndrome: slow thinking, poor judgement, decreased curiosity, social withdrawal, irritability, apathy that can explode into impulsive disinhibition).

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q25** - parietal tests include finger agnosia, astereognosis, dysgraphaesthesia, two-point discrimination and right-left orientation (lexical fluency is not one); Gerstmann syndrome is right-left disorientation, finger agnosia, dysgraphia and dyscalculia from a dominant parietal lesion.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q45** - patients with schizophrenia perform far worse than controls on the category test, Wisconsin card sort, speech sounds perception test and Trail B of the Halstead-Reitan battery, but overall cognitive ability tests such as the **MMSE** are usually intact.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q37** - the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (lateral Brodmann areas 9-12, 45, 46 and the upper area 47) is supplied by the middle cerebral artery, so its occlusion causes dorsolateral prefrontal dysfunction.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q94** - anterograde amnesia is the period of amnesia between an event (e.g. head injury) and the resumption of continuous memory; its length correlates with the extent of brain injury.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q96** - intellectual insight is admission that the patient is ill and that symptoms are caused by his own disturbances without applying this knowledge to future experience (agrees there is a problem, but takes no active steps).

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q68** - la belle indifference is an inappropriate lack of concern about a functional deficit or disability; part of classical descriptions of hysteria and conversion disorder, but also seen in medical illness (e.g. after a stroke) and of no diagnostic value.

blocks.note: Not in the notes: ideomotor apraxia is difficulty copying skilled movements - the patient knows what to do but not how, being unable to mimic a learned motor task such as combing hair - from damage to the dominant parietal lobe; abnormalities include abnormal amplitude, body-part-as-object substitution and abnormal orientation of body parts.

Not in the notes: personality change, sexual disinhibition and tremors suggest frontal lobe dementia, so the crucial history to elicit is the family history (strong family history in ==50%== of cases).

Not in the notes: in frontal-type dementia with disinhibition, lack of concern for others and recklessness, the language deficit expected first is non-fluent expressive dysphasia; the explanation lists reduced speech output, mutism, echolalia and perseveration among the language abnormalities.

Not in the notes: orientation is usually assessed to time, place and person; knowing today's date is the keyed test - time orientation is the most helpful (include the time of day), it is not particularly sensitive and intact orientation does not exclude a significant memory disorder, and being out by two days or less is considered normal when scoring formally.

Not in the notes. **Q47** **EEG** frequency bands (beta greater than 13 Hz; alpha 8-13 Hz; theta 4-7.5 Hz; delta 3.5 Hz or less).

blocks.note: Not in the notes (they cover QTc only): Mobitz type I **AV** block shows the **PR** interval lengthening progressively until one P wave fails to be conducted and produces no **QRS** complex, after which the **PR** interval resets and the cycle repeats.
Not in the notes: Mobitz type **II** block has a fixed, normal **PR** interval with an occasional P wave that fails to produce a **QRS** complex.

Not in the notes: in complete heart block there is complete interruption of conduction between atria and ventricles, so the P waves bear no relationship to the **QRS** complexes, which usually arise from a ventricular escape rhythm.

Not in the notes (**EMI**): difficulty recognising complex pictures though able to describe the parts = simultanagnosia; difficulty copying a wire cube = visuospatial agnosia; denial of left hemiplegia and gait disturbance after a stroke = anosognosia; failing to recognise the faces of children and close friends while recognising their voices = prosopagnosia; feeling that the limbs on one side of the body are missing = hemisomatognosia (a unilateral lack of body image that can occur in migraine or an epileptic aura).
