mindMap.label: History Taking & Interview Skills: tasks and non-directive techniques

children.label: Four tasks of the interview: build alliance, get demographics, interview for diagnosis, negotiate a treatment plan.
Threatening topics: normalizing questions, symptom expectation, symptom exaggeration, familiar language.
Open-ended questions open the interview and allow free narration; preferable when highly suggestible; poor use if over-talkative or extremely poor historian.
Repetition repeats the patient's exact words; restatement rearranges the phrasing; both show the doctor is listening actively.
Summation briefly summarises what the patient has said so far, letting the patient check it and helping the doctor form an idea of the narration.
Clarification seeks details of what the patient already said; facilitation uses verbal and nonverbal encouragement ('uh-huh', nods) to keep information flowing.

'Sometimes when people are very depressed, they think of hurting themselves' = normalisation; asking 'what sorts of drugs do you usually use' = symptom expectation; self-revelation can powerfully backfire.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/EMIS all chapters/EMIs Clinical Examination.pdf

children.label: Open questions give more informative answers than closed ones; begin open, then close to clarify details.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

children.label: Suggestive questions are the odd one out among techniques that facilitate disclosure.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

children.label: Repetition = the patient's exact words; restatement = rearranged phrases; summation = periodic summary that lets the patient clarify.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/EMIS all chapters/EMIs Clinical Examination.pdf

mindMap.label: Directive techniques and changing topics

children.label: Directive techniques seek a particular answer; not necessarily detrimental but must be used judiciously.
Three transitions: smooth (cue from what the patient just said), referred (cue from earlier in the interview), introduced (new topic from thin air).
Closed questions: yes/no answers; avoid early and in highly suggestible patients; start open and move to closed by the end; useful to rule out less likely symptoms.
Question rephrasing restates the question in different terms to collect specific information when the patient digresses.
Redirection gently reorients the patient to the topic to keep them on track.
Limit setting manages time pressure in garrulous patients; overuse may detach the patient from the doctor.
Referred transition = referring back to something said earlier in the interview.
Closed questions suit a distracted or over-talkative patient and ruling out symptoms, but are better avoided early and in suggestible patients.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

mindMap.label: Other methods to elicit information

children.label: Confrontation points out what the doctor thinks the patient is missing or denying; done respectfully to help the patient face a difficult aspect.
Interpretation clarifies associations the patient may not see; sophisticated, used after rapport, stated as a hypothesis.
Self-revelation is limited discreet self-disclosure; excessive self-revelation is a boundary violation.
Silence can facilitate discourse or indicate disapproval/disinterest; allows free emotional expression.
Symptom expectation: ask about details assuming the patient is involved in the behaviour, to defuse admission and reduce guilt.
Symptom exaggeration: overstate a guessed frequency when deception/minimisation is expected, to elicit the true answer.
Confrontation helps the patient face a difficult aspect of their problems.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

children.label: Interrupting 'there are few important things we need to cover' = limit setting; mentioning the doctor's own fandom = self-revelation.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/EMIS all chapters/EMIs Clinical Examination.pdf

mindMap.label: Supportive and obstructive techniques

children.label: Supportive (not information-eliciting): reassurance, advice, postponement, validation/normalisation, acknowledgement of affect, positive reinforcement, statement of respect, partnering.
Reassurance must not be falsely reassuring; premature advice can obstruct rather than facilitate.
Validation/normalisation quotes how normal different reactions are, to decrease embarrassment.
Statement of respect = genuine affirmative statements indicating respect and dignity with positive reinforcement.
Partnering: invite the patient's questions and concerns, encouraging team working.
Obstructive: suggestive, why and compound questions, negative nonverbal gestures, disapproval, setting traps.
Suggestive questions contain the answer in the question; compound questions confuse and give vague or no response.
Validation is the supportive technique not aimed at eliciting information.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

children.label: 'I am impressed by what you have achieved despite all these difficulties' = respectful statement.
Praising a patient who stopped mid-narration for doing well despite difficulty = reinforcement.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

mindMap.label: Open vs closed questions, difficult historians, ancillary methods and interpreters

children.label: Open questions: highly informative but low reliability, low precision, not time efficient; closed questions: low yield but reliable, precise, time efficient.
Poor historian: open-ended questions and commands, continuation techniques, shift to neutral ground, second interview as last resort.
Garrulous historian: closed and multiple-choice questions, gentle interruption, educate about moving along.
Behavioural observation: event sampling (every 5th/10th event coded) vs time sampling (every 5 or 10 minutes); often used in seclusion.
Functional (ABC) analysis observes antecedents, behaviour and consequences; used in LD, dementia care and challenging behaviour services.
Interpreters: brief them, insist on literal (not interpreted) translation in the MSE, debrief them, use the same one for a case.

mindMap.label: Laboratory assessment of physical factors: depression

children.label: Depression is a clinical diagnosis; examine physically (especially endocrine causes); labs if medical cause suspected and for baseline before antidepressants.
Chronic medical illnesses are associated with depression but do not 'present' as it, so they need not all be excluded.
Work-up tests: FBC, TSH, B12, HIV/syphilis if suspected, electrolytes, GFR/creatinine, LFTs, toxicology; urinary free cortisol for Cushing; ACTH stimulation for Addison's.
DST non-suppression rises from grief (10%) to dysthymia (23%), MDD (44%), melancholia (50%), psychotic affective (69%) and depression with serious suicidality (78%).
DST non-suppression is non-specific (chronic pain, eating disorders, alcoholism, OCD, anxiety); DST-positive patients respond better to biological treatments.
CRH test: blunted ACTH response; TRH test: about 30% show blunted TSH response.
Overt hypothyroidism in 1-4% of depressed patients; subclinical hypothyroidism in 4-40%, contributing to treatment failure.
TSH assay is the best screening test for subclinical hypothyroidism.
On lithium with TSH 6.4 and normal T4 (subclinical thyroid disease): repeat TSH in a month.

mindMap.label: Laboratory assessment: anxiety and other neuroses, lactate infusion and narcoanalysis

children.label: Medical causes of panic: paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, PE, seizures, Meniere's, TIA, carcinoid, Cushing's, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycaemia, phaeochromocytoma.
Examine all first presentations; extensive medical work-up only if features suggest physical disease.
Sodium lactate triggers panic in about 72% of panic disorder patients; blocked by benzodiazepines and tricyclics, not peripherally acting beta-blockers.
Amobarbital: organic muteness/stupor/catatonia worsens, psychogenic improves; therapeutic in repression and dissociation (amnesia, fugue); benzodiazepines can substitute.
Poor response to anxiolytic agents prompts a search for a medical cause of recurrent anxiety.
EMI: lactate = panic disorder; prolactin = pseudoseizure versus seizure; CPK = NMS; urinalysis = SIADH; DST = depression.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/EMIS all chapters/EMIs Clinical Examination.pdf

children.label: In narcoanalysis organic muteness does NOT improve with amobarbital; psychogenic muteness does.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

mindMap.label: Laboratory assessment: psychosis

children.label: Psychosis history: consider head trauma, seizures, headaches, focal deficits, abnormal movements, memory loss, drug use, and B12/folate/thiamine/niacin deficiencies.
Initial tests: FBC, thyroid profile, glucose/lipids/ECG, prolactin, electrolytes, GFR/creatinine, LFTs, toxicology.
Antipsychotic baselines: FBC (haemotoxic olanzapine/clozapine), glucose/lipids/ECG, prolactin, LFTs.
Toxic drug effects are the most common cause of psychosis; screen amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis, benzodiazepines.
Specific conditions: Wilson's - serum ceruloplasmin and 24-h copper excretion; hyperparathyroidism - calcium and PTH; Cushing's - 24-h urinary free cortisol then DST/ACTH challenge.
Suspected encephalitis: NMDAR and VGKC auto-antibodies; autoimmune screen: ANA, CRP, ESR.
AIP: abdominal pain, neuropathy, constipation, no rash; autosomal dominant, 18-40 years; triggered by oestrogens, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, diclofenac.
AIP key test: urinary porphobilinogen in acute attacks; treat with haemin.
Chronic subdural haematoma, not subarachnoid haemorrhage, fits insidious headache, fluctuating memory loss and unequal pupils.
Wing-beating tremor with memory loss and personality change = Wilson's disease: low serum ceruloplasmin.
Constipation, abdominal pain and hallucinations after hypnotics and diclofenac = acute intermittent porphyria: urine porphyrins.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

children.label: Chlorpromazine is the odd one out among drugs that increase urine porphyrins.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

mindMap.label: Autoimmune encephalitis presenting as psychosis (anti-NMDAR)

children.label: Receptors targeted by autoimmune psychosis: VGKC complex, NMDA, AMPA, GABA-B, glycine.
6.3% of first-onset psychosis patients have pathogenic antibodies against brain receptors; anti-NMDAR encephalitis is the best known.
Anti-NMDAR: 80% female, about 50% of women have ovarian teratoma, 75% first see a psychiatrist with psychosis/mania, about 4% purely psychiatric.
Investigate: serum NMDAR/VGKC antibodies, ANA/CRP/ESR/FBC/U+E (low sodium with anti-VGKC), EEG, MRI; confirm with CSF.
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, oligoclonal bands in about 60%; MRI normal in about 50%; pelvic US/CT in females.
Treatment: methylprednisolone then prednisolone plus plasma exchange; maintain with steroids, steroid-sparing agent or rituximab.
Avoid antipsychotics (dystonia, NMS-like syndrome); benzodiazepines may be needed.
Herpes encephalitis: lymphocytic CSF with red cells, temporal T2 hyperintensity and lateralised periodic EEG discharges.

mindMap.label: Laboratory assessment: dementia

children.label: Memory complaints: thorough physical examination for neurological signs; nutritional/metabolic causes can give 'reversible' dementia.
Initial work-up: FBC, thyroid profile, glucose/lipids/ECG, thiamine and folate, syphilis/HIV, electrolytes, GFR, LFTs, CT/MRI.
Thiamine deficiency can impair memory especially in alcoholics; low T4 can cause cognitive impairment.
HIV is associated with cognitive impairment that can worsen with opportunistic infections.
CT/MRI is routine but low-yield in Alzheimer's type; recommended if vascular dementia, subdural haematoma or tumour suspected.
No routine EEG; rapid-onset dementia may suggest CJD, warranting EEG and MRI.
Gene testing for Huntington's is essential without a family history but does not itself give a clinical diagnosis.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/Clinical Examination Attempt review.pdf

children.label: Mild cognitive impairment differs from dementia by preserved activities of daily living.

mindMap.label: Anorexia nervosa: investigations and BMI

children.label: Endocrine: low LH/FSH/oestradiol, low T3 with normal TSH, mildly raised cortisol, raised growth hormone, low leptin.
ECG: conduction defects, QT prolongation of major concern; GI: delayed gastric emptying, reduced colonic motility.
Haematology: normocytic normochromic anaemia, mild leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; metabolic: hypercholesterolaemia, raised carotene, hypophosphataemia, dehydration.
Vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia; laxative misuse causes metabolic acidosis, hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia.
Osteopenia/osteoporosis and pseudo-atrophy (enlarged ventricles and CSF spaces).
BMI = kg / m^2; underweight <18.5, normal 18.5-24.9, overweight 25-29.9, obese 30+.

mindMap.label: Alcohol use disorders: tests and complications

children.label: No single lab test diagnoses alcohol abuse; CDT is the most specific and sensitive for heavy use over the last 10 days, best compared with the patient's own baseline.
AUDIT is often considered the best screening tool in primary care.
Neurological complications: seizures, Wernicke's, Korsakoff's, polyneuropathy, cerebellar degeneration, Marchiafava syndrome.
GI: GI bleeds, Mallory-Weiss tears, fatty liver, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, pancreatitis, hypoglycaemia; cardiac: cardiomyopathy, hypertension.
Haematologic: pancytopenia, folate/B12 deficiency with MCV changes, clotting disorders; renal: hepatorenal syndrome, hyponatraemia.
Pregnancy: low birth weight, foetal alcohol syndrome, developmental delay, neural tube defects.
EMI: GGT = sensitive marker; CDT = recent abuse and relapse; MCV = more specific; AUDIT = best primary-care screen.

children.label: Confused alcoholic after surgery: petechial rash = septicaemia; nystagmus = Wernicke; flapping tremor = hepatic failure.

mindMap.label: Specific investigations: ECG/QTc and urine drug testing

children.label: ECG on psychiatric wards mainly measures QT when using antipsychotics; prolonged QT risks torsades de pointes.
QTc risk: beyond 440 ms (men) / 470 ms (women); over 500 ms clearly increased risk; QTc has low positive predictive value.
QTc risk factors include hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia, heart disease, female sex, extremes of age, liver disease, stimulants, starvation, high dose.
Check urine specific gravity to detect tap-water adulteration of drug-test samples.

Urine detection: alcohol up to 12 h, amphetamine up to 48 h, benzodiazepine 3 days, cocaine 6-8 h (metabolites 2-4 days), heroin 1-3 days, morphine 2-3 days, codeine 48 h, methadone 3+ days, PCP 8 days.
Cannabis in urine: up to 3 days occasional use; up to 4 weeks high daily long-term use.

mindMap.label: Renal disturbances, SIADH, polydipsia and diabetes insipidus

children.label: Heroin user with puffy face, hypertension and weight gain: suspect heroin-related nephropathy; FSGS often in Black patients, membranoproliferative GN in Whites.
Urine analysis matters for SIADH (antidepressants/antipsychotics), psychogenic polydipsia and DI (lithium nephrogenic; head injury central).
Osmolality guide: plasma high + urine low = DI; plasma low + urine low = psychogenic polydipsia; plasma low + urine high = SIADH.
Polydipsia: gradual onset, rare nocturia, normal/low plasma osmolality; DI: acute onset, common nocturia, elevated plasma osmolality.
Polydipsia and polyuria are not features of SIADH or hyponatraemia per se.
Hyponatraemia is mostly asymptomatic until sodium below 125 mmol/L; below 110-115 mmol/L seizures and irreversible brain damage can occur.
Puffy face, weight gain and hypertension in an intravenous heroin user = heroin-associated nephropathy.

children.label: Low urine and plasma osmolality with polyuria and polydipsia = psychogenic polydipsia.

children.label: Water intoxication: tremor, ataxia, vomiting, diarrhoea and polyuria - ask about water drinking.

mindMap.label: Physical examination of a psychiatric patient: general examination

children.label: Pupils: Argyll-Robertson - neurosyphilis (diabetes more common cause); constricted - opiate intoxication/Horner's; dilated - stimulant abuse, opiate withdrawal, anxiety.
Signs: checker-board abdomen = factitious disorder; Kayser-Fleischer ring = Wilson's; lymph nodes = HIV/lymphoma; lanugo = anorexia; Russell's sign = bulimia.
Parotid swelling: bulimia, mumps; sialorrhoea: clozapine, parkinsonism, Bell's palsy, stroke; xanthelasma: olanzapine/antipsychotic.
Cushing's: lemon-on-stick appearance, central obesity; hyperthyroid: lid lag, retraction, exophthalmos, proptosis; piloerection: opiate withdrawal.
Hyperventilation: tachypnoea, carpopedal spasm, paraesthesias (acid-base imbalance; usually bilateral, perioral numbness common).
Minor physical anomalies are more frequent in patients with schizophrenia and their siblings, supporting neurodevelopmental aetiology; rated with the Lane Scale.
Multiple abdominal scars ('checker-board abdomen') = factitious disorder.

mindMap.label: Neurological examination: cranial nerves, hearing and vestibular tests

children.label: Cranial nerves I-XII with bedside tests: smell, acuity/fields/pupils, eye movements, facial and corneal sensation, facial movement, balance/hearing, palate/cough, shrug, tongue.
CN II fields are tested by confrontation/perimetry, colour by Ishihara, acuity by Snellen.
CN VIII: vestibular - Romberg/caloric; cochlear - Rinne and Weber.
Weber: louder in the abnormal ear in conductive loss; lateralises to the normal ear in sensorineural loss.
Rinne: in conductive loss bone conduction exceeds air conduction; in sensorineural loss both are reduced similarly.
Romberg: patient falls to the side of vestibular hypofunction; also positive in polyneuropathy and dorsal column disease but without consistent side.
Caloric mnemonic COWS: cold - opposite, warm - same.
The confrontation test assesses visual fields (optic tract lesions).

children.label: Bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia is the eye sign pathognomonic of multiple sclerosis.

mindMap.label: Neurological soft signs and cerebellar signs

children.label: Hard signs are localisable motor/sensory deficits; soft signs are non-localisable, thought to reflect neurodevelopmental aberration (schizophrenia, autism, OCD, ADHD).
Soft signs group into motor coordination, sensory integration and cortical disinhibition abnormalities; the hard/soft distinction is artificial.
Cerebellar anatomy: lateral hemispheres - ipsilateral limbs; vermis - truncal tone, speech, eye movements; flocculonodular lobe - vestibular.
Cerebellar signs: ataxia, hypotonia, intention tremor, dyssynergia, dysmetria (past pointing).
More cerebellar signs: dysdiadochokinesis, dysrhythmia, dysarthria (staccato/scanning speech, diffuse involvement).
Finger-nose or heel-shin tests elicit dyssynergia, dysmetria and tremor.
Ankle clonus is the odd one out among cerebellar signs.

children.label: Pupillary mydriasis is not cerebellar; it occurs in severe alcohol withdrawal (DTs).

mindMap.label: Meningeal signs, cortical sensory signs and movement abnormalities

children.label: Meningeal signs arise with meningeal inflammation or irritation (including haemorrhage/trauma).
Brudzinski: neck flexion causes hip/knee flexion; Kernig: extending the knee with hip flexed gives hamstring spasm.
Lasegue SLR limitation = lower lumbar root irritation; reverse SLR (prone) limitation = upper lumbar root irritation.
Asterixis (wrists dorsiflexed, palms forward): jerky downward wrist movements, metabolic encephalopathy; pronator drift (palms up): hemiparetic weakness.
Chorea - caudate lesions; hemiballismus - subthalamic nucleus lesions; myoclonus - <0.25 s jerk, CJD and severe Alzheimer's.
Fasciculations usually benign but if widespread may indicate neuromuscular disease such as ALS.
Left arm drifting down on the palms-up arms-outstretched test = right cerebral hemisphere lesion.

children.label: To tell lithium from risperidone tremor, examine tone: EPSE gives tremor and rigidity, lithium tremor does not.

mindMap.label: Reflexes, neurocutaneous signs and speech abnormalities

children.label: Primitive reflexes (glabellar, rooting, snout, sucking, palmomental) are absent in adults; their presence signals diffuse frontal damage (frontal-release signs).
Superficial reflexes: corneal, conjunctival, abdominal, cremasteric, plantar; corneal afferent via CN V, efferent via CN VII.
Positive Babinski (great toe dorsiflexion) suggests UMN lesion; normal is plantar flexion.
Deep tendon reflexes: exaggerated in UMN lesions, absent in LMN lesions; roots: biceps C5-6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, patellar L2-4, Achilles S4.

Neurocutaneous: ash leaf macules and ungual fibromas - tuberous sclerosis; cafe au lait spots - neurofibromata/tuberous sclerosis; axillary freckling - neurofibroma; frontal baldness - myotonic dystrophy.
Dysarthria: spastic (bilateral UMN), flaccid (LMN), ataxic (scanning, cerebellar), hypokinetic (breathy monotone), hyperkinetic (basal ganglia), mixed.
Hysterical aphonia: sudden voice loss with normal examination and preserved vocal cord activity.
The cremasteric reflex is a superficial reflex, not a frontal release sign.

mindMap.label: Gait

children.label: Hemiparetic gait: stroke; clenched hand, extended knee, circumduction of the paralysed leg.
Ataxic gait: wide-based staggering; unilateral cerebellar lesion veers to the side of the lesion (sailor's gait).
Shuffling/festinating gait: Parkinson's; short accelerating steps.
Steppage gait: foot drop, peripheral neuropathy, dorsal column disorders; waddling: proximal myopathy, pregnancy; scissoring: spastic paraplegia.
Gait apraxia (magnetic gait) - hydrocephalus; lurching chaotic - Huntington's; propulsive - carbon monoxide poisoning; stomping - Friedreich's/tabes dorsalis/pernicious anaemia.
Trendelenburg gait: weak hip abductors, principally gluteus medius.
EMI gaits: Huntington = lurching; pregnancy = waddling; hip dysplasia = pigeon; Friedreich ataxia = stomping.

mindMap.label: Other neurological signs and eponyms

children.label: Absent ankle jerks with upgoing plantars: subacute combined degeneration, taboparesis, Friedreich's ataxia, MND.
Pupils: Horner = small, reacts to light; tonic pupil = parasympathetic; Argyll-Robertson = small, irregular, accommodates but no light reaction.
Brown-Sequard: ipsilateral spastic paralysis, Babinski and loss of fine touch/vibration/position; contralateral pain and temperature loss 2-3 segments below.
Horner's syndrome (PAMELA) = same-sided sympathetic lesion e.g. apical lung tumour, carotid aneurysm; Marcus-Gunn = afferent pupillary defect on swinging flashlight.
Holmes-Adie: tonic pupil with absent patellar and Achilles reflexes; Chvostek: hypocalcaemia; Gower: severe myopathy; Friedreich's: pes cavus, kyphoscoliosis, cardiomyopathy.
Optic neuritis triad: vision loss, eye pain, dyschromatopsia; Uhthoff symptom in 50%; afferent pupillary defect.
Subacute combined degeneration is due to B12 deficiency; milkmaid's grip and trombone tongue occur in chorea.
Normal accommodation but no light reflex = Argyll-Robertson pupil.

mindMap.label: UMN vs LMN lesions; bulbar vs pseudobulbar palsy

children.label: UMN lesion: hypertonia/rigidity, exaggerated reflexes, mild disuse atrophy; LMN lesion: hypotonia, absent reflexes, wasting, fasciculations.
Bulbar palsy: LMN lesion of CN 9-12; wasted fasciculating tongue, nasal speech, lost jaw jerk and gag, no emotional lability.
Pseudobulbar palsy: bilateral UMN lesions; stiff tongue, Donald-duck speech, exaggerated jaw jerk, preserved gag, emotional lability.
Bulbar causes: MND, polio, botulism, myasthenia gravis, muscular dystrophy; pseudobulbar causes: MND, MS, multi-infarct dementia, severe head injury.
Muscle atrophy is seen in LMN lesions, not UMN lesions.

mindMap.label: Bedside cognitive examination tools

children.label: MMSE: 30 points, 5-10 minutes; cut-off 21/22 if under 9 years of education (usual 23/24); misses early decline and frontal executive defects.
MMSE items: orientation 10, registration and recall 6, attention 5, command 3, naming 2, repetition 1, reading 1, writing 1, visual construction 1.
Clock drawing needs comprehension, working memory, spatial knowledge, constructional skill and executive planning; it does NOT test orientation to time.
Watson clock score 0-3 normal; 4 or more: sensitivity 87%, specificity 82%.
ACE-R: six domains; more sensitive to frontal dementias than MMSE; cut-offs <88 and <82; language carries most of the score.
Overreliance on MMSE scores can be counterproductive; the clinical interview with carers and patients is the best diagnostic tool.
The clinical interview of patient and carer is the most useful tool for diagnosing dementia.
The clock-drawing test does not assess orientation to time.

children.label: The Addenbrooke's cognitive examination is the tool for global cognitive functioning.
ACE-R below 82 has high specificity (1.0) with sensitivity 0.84.

mindMap.label: Imaging of the nervous system: CT and MRI

children.label: CT: most widely available, quick, cheap, but radiation; poor for early ischaemia, posterior fossa and structures near bone; calcification better seen than on MRI.
MRI: no radiation, good for early ischaemia and posterior fossa; limited availability, longer, costlier; contraindicated with pacemakers/ferromagnetic implants.
T1: fat bright, CSF dark, best for structure, only sequence with gadolinium contrast; T2: CSF white, pathology (water) bright, best for pathology.
FLAIR detects hippocampal sclerosis in temporal lobe epilepsy; proton density shows periventricular structures.
Infarct, tumour, MS plaque and CSF are dark on CT and T1 but bright on T2; haemorrhage bright on CT, T1 and T2 (unless too old/too fresh).
Bone is bright on CT and T1 but dark on T2; air dark on all; fat dark on CT but bright on T1 and T2.
Delayed deterioration after a blow to the head: CT, not X-ray or MRI, for fresh haemorrhage.

mindMap.label: Magnetic resonance spectroscopy and functional MRI

children.label: MRS detects odd-numbered nuclei; 1H quantifies NAA, creatine, choline; GABA and glutamate detectable but not dopamine (too low concentration).
31P MRS measures brain pH and phosphorus compounds (ATP, GTP).
Nuclei uses: 19F - pO2, glucose metabolism, pH, pharmacokinetics; 7Li - pharmacokinetics; 14N - glutamate, urea, ammonia; 13C - metabolite turnover; 17O - metabolic rate.
MRS can measure brain lithium; fluoxetine and trifluoperazine contain fluorine-19 and are detectable.
fMRI uses BOLD: deoxyhaemoglobin is paramagnetic, detected on T2; it is a proxy of perfusion, not neuronal metabolism.
fMRI uses no radioactive isotopes (advantage over PET and SPECT); resting fMRI maps the default mode network (precuneus, lateral parietal, medial prefrontal).

mindMap.label: SPECT, PET and diffusion tensor imaging

children.label: SPECT: single-photon isotopes (I-123, Tc-99m, Xe-133) measure regional blood flow, not neuronal metabolism directly.
Xenon-133 SPECT (rCBF) measures only surface blood flow; Tc-99m HMPAO gives whole-brain perfusion and is most used in dementia.
SPECT ligands: iodobenzamide - D1/D2; iomazenil - GABA-A; nor-beta-CIT - dopamine/serotonin transporters; epidepride - D2/D3.
PET emits two particles (SPECT one): better localisation and resolution (closer to 3 mm); needs an on-site cyclotron.
FDG (18F-fluorodeoxyglucose) is the most used PET ligand and gives direct information about neuronal metabolism.
PET ligands: raclopride - D2; flumazenil - GABA-A; altanserin/setoperone - 5HT2; methyltryptophan - serotonin synthesis; scopolamine - muscarinic; 18F dopa - dopamine neuron density.
DTI: fractional anisotropy indexes white matter integrity; tractography infers white-matter connectivity.
PET gives metabolic information; SPECT gives blood flow only.

mindMap.label: Neuroimaging findings in psychiatry

children.label: Depression: periventricular/deep WM and thalamic/striatal hyperintensities; reduced frontal and basal ganglia volumes; lower prefrontal, cingulate, amygdala metabolism.
Depression: higher anterior cingulate/prefrontal metabolism predicts better treatment response; higher 5HT2A density, raised MAO-A, raised D2 binding (psychomotor retardation).
Therapeutic SSRI dose occupies 80% of 5HT transporters.
Schizophrenia: ventricular enlargement; grey matter loss (insula, anterior cingulate, medial temporal); progressive volume loss in first years; poor DLPFC activation; low NAA in PFC; reduced FA.
Alzheimer's: ventricular enlargement, loss of temporal volume especially hippocampus, reduced parieto-temporal fMRI activation and SPECT flow.
OCD: caudate volumes reduced and increased reported; higher caudate blood flow that falls with effective treatment.
Insula shows unequivocal volumetric abnormality in schizophrenia.
